```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.authoring import data_card, excerpt, lesson_header, reproduce_this
from pbc.electromagnetism import two_port
from pbc.electromagnetism.experiments import microwave_sparameter_lab as experiment

result = experiment.run()
lesson_header()
```

The RLC lesson gave a resistor, a coil, and a capacitor their impedances;
the waveguide lesson showed a wave that travels along a guide and only
changes its phase. At tens of gigahertz an electrical part is measured with
both ideas at once: a vector network analyser sends a wave into one port of
the part and records the complex amplitudes of the waves that come back and
that come out of the other port. Their ratios are the scattering parameters,
or S-parameters, of the part.

The National Physical Laboratory measured three small attenuators on a
wafer, labelled [3 dB]{.given}, [6 dB]{.given}, and
[10 dB]{.given} pads, with two different analysers, and published the
calibrated files. How much of the power that enters each pad comes out,
how much is reflected, and how much stays in it? Does a model of a few
resistors and inductors, with a short line on either side, describe the
measured amplitudes, and up to which frequency? And how well does the record
itself say these numbers are known?

## Assumptions

1. **The calibration is the creators'.** The files are corrected by a
   multiline TRL calibration (thru, reflect, line), applied by the creators,
   which sets the reference planes at which the S-parameters are stated;
   the files do not say where they lie. The calibration standards and the
   uncertainty of the calibration are
   described in the conference paper the record supports, not in the files;
   this lab does not use that paper and states no calibration uncertainty.
2. **A reference impedance.** Every S-parameter is a ratio of waves on lines of
   the reference impedance the files state, [50 Ω]{.given}.
3. **Linear and time-invariant.** The analyser measures one frequency at a
   time with a small signal; the pads are assumed to respond in proportion
   and not to change between sweeps. The data cannot test linearity.
4. **The fitted band.** Every model of this page is fitted between `{python} result["f-min"]` and
   `{python} result["coax-max"]` GHz, the band of the coaxial system; above it the model is a
   prediction tested against the single sweep.
5. **No uncertainty per point.** The files give none. The fitted values
   carry standard errors from the scatter of the residuals, which assume
   independent residuals; the lab checks that assumption and finds it
   false.

## Explanation {#explanation}

### Waves in, waves out

On a line of impedance $Z_0$, a voltage and a current at one place are the
sum of a wave going in and a wave coming out. At port $j$ of a two-port the
analyser calls the incoming wave $a_j$ and the outgoing wave $b_j$, scaled
so that $|a_j|^2$ is the power the wave carries. A linear two-port relates
them by a matrix of complex numbers,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} b_1 \\ b_2 \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} S_{11} & S_{12} \\ S_{21} & S_{22} \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ a_2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$

With nothing sent into port $2$ and port $2$ terminated in $Z_0$, $S_{11}$ is
the reflection at port $1$ and $S_{21}$ the transmission from port $1$ to
port $2$. Each is an amplitude ratio with a modulus and a phase.

### Amplitude, power, and decibels

The power of a wave goes with the square of its amplitude, so the fraction
of the incident power that leaves port $2$ is $|S_{21}|^2$ and the fraction
reflected is $|S_{11}|^2$. A decibel is a power ratio,

$$
L = -10 \log_{10} |S_{21}|^2 = -20 \log_{10} |S_{21}|,
$$

the same number written either way. A pad of exactly [3 dB]{.given} passes half the
power and $1/\sqrt{2}$ of the amplitude. The common slip is to take ten
times the logarithm of the amplitude, which halves every loss.

### Energy and passivity

The power that enters port $1$ either comes back, goes out of port $2$, or stays
in the part as heat:

$$
1 - |S_{11}|^2 - |S_{21}|^2 \ \ge\ 0
$$

for a part with no source of energy inside, and zero for a lossless one.
The same holds for port $2$ and for any combination of waves sent in at both
ports at once, which is the statement that the largest singular value of
the matrix $S$ is at most one. A reciprocal part, of resistors, coils, and
capacitors, has $S_{21} = S_{12}$; a symmetric one also has
$S_{11} = S_{22}$.

### A pad of lumped elements between two lines

A resistive T pad is three resistors: one in series on each side and one
across the middle to ground. With the element impedances of the RLC lesson,
an arm is $Z_\text{arm} = R_\text{series} + j\omega L$ (a resistor with an
inductance in series) and the middle is $R_\text{shunt}$. The
impedance parameters of the symmetric T are $Z_{11} = Z_\text{arm} +
R_\text{shunt}$ and $Z_{21} = R_\text{shunt}$, and the S-parameters follow
from them:

$$
S_{11} = \frac{(Z_{11} - Z_0)(Z_{11} + Z_0) - Z_{21}^2}{(Z_{11} + Z_0)^2 - Z_{21}^2},
\qquad
S_{21} = \frac{2 Z_{21} Z_0}{(Z_{11} + Z_0)^2 - Z_{21}^2}.
$$

The pad is matched, $S_{11} = 0$, when $R_\text{series} = Z_0 (k-1)/(k+1)$
and $R_\text{shunt} = 2 Z_0 k/(k^2 - 1)$ with $k = 10^{L/20}$. The
reference planes of the calibration need not be at the resistors: there
may be a length of line between each plane and the pad. The waveguide lesson
gave a guided wave the factor $e^{-j\beta z}$; a line with no cut-off
carries a wave at a fixed speed $v$, so $\beta = \omega / v$ and a matched
line of length $\ell$ only delays the wave by $\tau = \ell / v$. The two
lines together multiply $S_{11}$ and $S_{21}$ by $e^{-j\omega\tau}$. The
model has four values: $R_\text{series}$, $R_\text{shunt}$, $L$, and
$\tau$. It is an equivalent circuit, not a drawing of the layout: a pi
network of three other values gives the same S-parameters.

### The Smith chart

A reflection coefficient $\Gamma = S_{11}$ and the impedance $Z$ that the
port presents are two descriptions of the same thing,

$$
z = \frac{Z}{Z_0} = \frac{1 + \Gamma}{1 - \Gamma},
\qquad
\Gamma = \frac{z - 1}{z + 1}.
$$

The Smith chart draws $\Gamma$ in its complex plane, inside the unit circle
for a passive port, with the lines of constant resistance $r = \mathrm{Re}\,z$
(circles) and constant reactance $x = \mathrm{Im}\,z$ (arcs) mapped onto it.
The centre is a perfect match; a point above the real axis is inductive, a
point below capacitive; a delay turns a point clockwise about the centre.

end of the band, and these data do not say whether the cause is in the pads
or in the calibration.

### What the standard errors assume

The standard errors of the fit table assume that the residuals at different
frequencies are independent. The last column of the residuals table checks it: the residuals at
neighbouring frequencies correlate at `{python} result["correlation-low"]`
to `{python} result["correlation-high"]`, far from zero. A residual that
moves smoothly with frequency counts as `{python} result["coax-points"]`
independent samples in the standard error when the data hold far fewer
independent pieces of information, so the standard errors are too small, and the lab does not use them as
uncertainties.

### What the lab shows

The three pads are passive at every measured frequency, absorb most of the
power that is not transmitted, and lose more than their labels say. A model
of four values, resistors and an inductance from the RLC lesson between
matched lines from the waveguide lesson, describes their complex
S-parameters between `{python} result["f-min"]` and `{python} result["coax-max"]` GHz with an rms residual of a few
thousandths and a largest misfit of `{python} result["misfit-max"]`, at the
lowest frequency; the same model fitted to one pad drifts away from the
measurement of that pad above `{python} result["coax-max"]` GHz. The record's two instruments agree on one pad to
`{python} result["instrument-db"]` dB in $|S_{21}|$, which bounds the
difference between the systems; no number on this page bounds the error of
the calibration itself.

## Limits {#limits}

- **No calibration uncertainty.** The files carry none; the paper the record
  supports describes the calibration and its uncertainty, and this lab does
  not use it. The instruments' difference bounds only what differs between
  the two systems.
- **One pad measured twice.** Only the [3 dB]{.given} pad has a second measurement, so
  the [6 dB]{.given} and [10 dB]{.given} pads have no cross-check, and nothing is known about
  repeated measurements with the same instrument.
- **An equivalent circuit.** The T network is one of many circuits with the
  same S-parameters; its values are not the resistors on the wafer, and the
  delay $\tau$ is not a measured line length.
- **Correlated residuals.** The standard errors of the fit assume
  independent residuals, which the data refute; the instrument and band
  fits are a sensitivity, not an interval.
- **A lumped model.** It holds to `{python} result["coax-max"]` GHz on this record and not to `{python} result["single-max"]` GHz;
  its structured misfit at the lowest frequencies is not explained.
- **The labels.** The pads are named by their nominal loss; the record does
  not state their tolerance.

about a hundredth of an ohm, and the fit on the other instrument's file
differs by almost five hundredths. Which number says more about how well
the record fixes $R_\text{series}$, and why is neither a full uncertainty?

::: {.solution}
The difference between the instruments says more. The standard error
assumes independent residuals, and the residuals of neighbouring
frequencies are strongly correlated, so it counts far too many independent
samples and comes out too small. The fit on the other instrument shows how
much the value moves when the measurement system changes. Neither is a full
uncertainty: both rest on the same model, and neither includes an error the
two calibrations share.
:::
:::
